content: Serious and potentially fatal hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in patients undergoing penicillin therapy. While anaphylaxis is more commonly associated with parenteral administration, it has also been observed in patients taking oral penicillins. These reactions are more likely to occur in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens. There are documented cases of individuals with penicillin hypersensitivity experiencing severe allergic reactions when treated with cephalosporins. Prior to initiating penicillin therapy, a thorough assessment of the patient’s history of hypersensitivity to penicillins, cephalosporins, and other allergens should be conducted. If an allergic reaction occurs, the medication must be discontinued immediately, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Severe anaphylactoid reactions require urgent emergency intervention, including the administration of epinephrine, oxygen, intravenous corticosteroids, and airway management, such as intubation, as clinically indicated. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with the use of nearly all antibacterial agents, including ampicillin. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to life-threatening colitis. Antibiotic treatment disrupts the normal gut flora, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile. The toxins produced by C. difficile, particularly toxins A and B, contribute to the development of CDAD. Hypervirulent strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may not respond to standard antimicrobial therapy and could necessitate surgical intervention, such as colectomy. CDAD should be considered in any patient presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even if the symptoms occur up to two months after the last dose. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotics not targeting C. difficile may be necessary. Supportive care, including fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation, should be implemented as clinically appropriate. During ampicillin therapy, there is a risk of superinfections caused by fungal or bacterial pathogens. If such infections occur, the drug should be discontinued, and alternative treatment should be initiated. A significant proportion (43–100%) of patients with infectious mononucleosis who receive ampicillin develop a skin rash. This rash typically appears 7–10 days after starting oral ampicillin and resolves within a few days to a week after discontinuation of the drug. The rash is generally maculopapular, pruritic, and widespread. Consequently, ampicillin is not recommended for patients with mononucleosis. It remains unclear whether these patients are truly allergic to ampicillin. Ampicillin should only be prescribed when there is a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a valid prophylactic indication. Prescribing it in the absence of such conditions is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Patients should be informed that antibacterial drugs, including ampicillin, are only effective against bacterial infections and do not treat viral infections, such as the common cold. When prescribed ampicillin, patients should be advised to adhere strictly to the prescribed regimen, even if they feel better early in the course of treatment. Skipping doses or failing to complete the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of the treatment and increase the risk of bacterial resistance, rendering the infection untreatable with ampicillin or other antibiotics in the future. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and typically resolves after discontinuation of the medication. However, patients should be advised to contact their physician immediately if they develop watery or bloody stools, with or without abdominal cramps and fever, even if these symptoms occur two or more months after completing antibiotic therapy. For patients undergoing prolonged therapy with ampicillin, periodic monitoring of organ function, including renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic systems, is recommended. Transient elevations in serum transaminase levels have been observed following ampicillin administration, though the clinical significance of this finding is unclear. Concurrent use of allopurinol with ampicillin significantly increases the incidence of skin rashes compared to ampicillin alone. It is uncertain whether this interaction is due to allopurinol itself or the underlying hyperuricemia in these patients. High concentrations of ampicillin in the urine may result in false-positive glucose test results when using methods such as Clinitest, Benedict’s Solution, or Fehling’s Solution. Therefore, glucose tests based on enzymatic glucose oxidase reactions, such as Clinistix or Tes-Tape, are recommended. No long-term animal studies have been conducted with ampicillin. Reproductive studies in animals at doses several times higher than the human dose have not shown evidence of adverse effects. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Since animal studies are not always predictive of human outcomes, ampicillin should only be used during pregnancy if clearly necessary. Oral ampicillin-class antibiotics are poorly absorbed during labor. Studies in guinea pigs have shown that intravenous ampicillin slightly decreases uterine tone and contraction frequency while moderately increasing contraction height and duration. It is unknown whether these effects occur in humans or whether ampicillin use during labor or delivery has immediate or delayed adverse effects on the fetus, prolongs labor, or increases the need for obstetric interventions or neonatal resuscitation. Ampicillin is excreted in trace amounts in human breast milk. Therefore, caution should be exercised when administering ampicillin-class antibiotics to nursing mothers. Guidelines for pediatric administration are provided in the Dosage and Administration section.
